newsitem.title: THAILAND: Lingering concerns grip Thai stocks, baht steady.
newsitem.headline: Lingering concerns grip Thai stocks, baht steady.

text.p: Thai stocks were still gripped by concerns over the troubled financial sector on Wednesday, with the benchmark SET index falling over two percent in the morning session, while the baht remained stable.

Concerns that more finance companies might be suspended led investors to sell stocks, especially of finance firms, driving the SET index to 631.19 by the midday break, down 17.28 points, or 2.66 percent, from the Tuesday close.
The index fell as low as 624.55 in the morning.
Sentiment was hurt by Tuesday's announcement by the central bank that it had suspended more than half of the country's finance firms.
The number of finance firms whose operations were suspended grew to 58 out of the nation's total of 91 finance firms.

"Investor worries that more finance companies might be suspended came after the government yesterday ordered operations of 42 finance firms suspended," said Thanawat Patchimkul, a trader of Seamico Securities Co Ltd.
Brokers said the market would be affected for the next few days as a result of the suspension as well as the implementation of monetary and fiscal measures aimed at healing the economy.

On the currency front, selling pressure on the Thai baht calmed somewhat in the domestic market on Wednesday. The baht traded at 31.60/70 to the dollar as of 0530 GMT in the domestic market, compared with 31.70/32.00 late on Tuesday.
In the offshore market, the baht gained sharply against the dollar as the currency's sentiment improved as a result of the economic package, dealers said. It was quoted at around 31.03/31.13.
"There were both bids and offers for the dollar in the market this morning. The dollar buying was easing quite a bit," said one dealer at a European bank.

Analysts largely welcomed the economic measures. The package, which was recommended by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), is expected to pave the way for a rescue loan package worth up to $15 billion by the IMF and foreign nations to help Thailand overcome its economic difficulties.
The package gained high marks from Washington and Tokyo, but questions remain over when and how the rescue package will be in place.

In Tokyo, an official of the Ministry of Finance told reporters on Wednesday that Japan ought to make the biggest contribution among foreign countries to the international package, but stopped well short of saying the amount of support to be provided by Tokyo.

More time will be needed before Thailand sees the return of foreign capital to the baht, which has plunged by about 20 percent since Bangkok allowed a de facto devaluation of the currency on July 2, analysts say.
They added that it largely hinged on how successful Bangkok was in implementing the new measures.
